Chapter 21

Forms that work without JavaScript

form(), fields.<name>.as(), and the rule that catches everybody once.

By the end of this chapter

A booking form that submits, validates and reports errors with scripting disabled — then gets better with it on.

form() is the third kind of remote function. It takes a schema and a handler, and the object it returns is spread straight onto a <form> element.

With JavaScript off this is an ordinary HTML form: it posts, the server validates, and the page comes back with errors filled in. With JavaScript on, SvelteKit intercepts, posts in the background, and updates in place. Same code, same handler, same validation.

Every input is spread from book.fields, including the three hidden ones that say which studio, which service and which time zone the booking is for. book.pending counts the submissions still in flight, which is what lets the button show it is working without a $state flag of your own.

A field that wires itself

The name input sits inside <Field>, and the {id}, describedBy and invalid it uses come from there. Field is this app's one form-field component, and it exists because a usable field needs three invisible things to be right at once: a label joined to its control, an error that is part of the control's description, and the control saying it is invalid.

The control itself is passed in as a snippet with parameters. children is typed Snippet<[{ id; describedBy; invalid }]>, Field renders it with {@render children({ id, describedBy, invalid: Boolean(error) })}, and the page receives those values by destructuring them in {#snippet children({ id, describedBy, invalid })}. So Field decides the ids, and the page decides what the control is: an <input>, a <textarea>, a <select>, each spread from its own fields.<name>.as(...).

Why a snippet, and why $props.id()

A snippet with parameters is Svelte 5's replacement for slot props — the let:id directive on a <slot> in Svelte 4 — and it is better in the way that matters here: it is typed. Destructure a name Field does not pass and TypeScript says so. The ids come from $props.id(), which gives each component instance a unique id that is the same on the server and in the browser. crypto.randomUUID() would produce one id in the server's HTML and another during hydration, and the label would end up pointing at nothing; a hard-coded id breaks the moment two fields on one page share it. Chapter 32 has the component test that holds all of this in place.

The rule that catches everybody once

Every control inside a remote form must come from fields.<name>.as(...). A hand-written <input type="hidden" name="slug"> throws "Form contained a field that wasn't created with form.fields.as(...)" the moment the form is submitted.

SvelteKit has to own the name and the value in order to construct the submitted object and match it against your schema. A field it did not create is a field it cannot account for, so it refuses rather than silently dropping it.

The second argument is the value. It caught us three times in this project: the booking page's service id, the slot grid's chosen time, and the sign-in page's redirectTo. The last one only broke sign-ins that arrived with a redirect, which meant every test that started at /manage failed and every test that started at /sign-in passed.

Showing what went wrong

  • fields.email.issues() — problems with that one field, shown next to it by Field.
  • formIssues — the problems that belong to the form as a whole rather than to any single input, such as a refused password. Worked out in the script, below.
  • aria-invalid and aria-describedby are what make the error readable rather than merely visible. A screen reader announces "Email, invalid entry, that does not look like an email address" instead of "Email, edit text".

fields.allIssues() is every issue in the form, the email's own included. The alert used to be built straight from it, so an email the schema rejected said "Enter the email address you signed up with" twice — once beside the field, once in the alert — in two role="alert" regions, both read aloud. Each issue carries a path to the field it belongs to, and an issue for the form as a whole has an empty one, so filtering on path.length === 0 leaves exactly the refusals the alert is for.

A refusal that belongs to the form

Schema issues land in those slots by themselves. A wrong password is different: the schema cannot know it. Only Better Auth can, after the submission has passed validation, so the handler has to report it itself, and the way it reports it decides what the person sees next.

invalid comes from @sveltejs/kit and throws, as error and redirect do. Given a plain string, it records an issue for the form as a whole — one with an empty path — which formIssues picks out for the "We could not sign you in" alert above, with the email still filled in. Given issue.email('…'), built from the second argument every form handler receives, it attaches to that one field instead.

Only one failure is a refusal, though. Better Auth throws an APIError with status 401 for a wrong password and for an unknown email alike — one message for both, which is what stops the form from telling a stranger which addresses have accounts. Everything else is rethrown. An earlier version caught everything with a bare catch {, which turned a database outage into "that password is wrong": no log line, no reference id, and somebody retyping a correct password at a server that could not read it. Rethrown, the outage reaches handleError as unknown, which logs it and shows the generic sentence.

Why not error(401, …)

This handler used to call error(401, 'That email and password do not match an account.'), and it looked fine, because the sentence appeared. But error inside a form handler sends the request to the nearest +error.svelte, which replaces the page. The form went, the email went with it, and somebody who had mistyped one character was looking at a failure screen. A wrong password is put right on the same form, a moment later, so the answer belongs on the form. The end-to-end test for a wrong password now checks that the form, and the email in it, are still there.

The underscore is the other half, and it matters most with JavaScript off. A submission that fails comes back as a freshly rendered page with every field filled in again, so nobody retypes their email. For a field called password, that means the wrong guess travels back across the network inside the input's value, in the HTML. SvelteKit never sends back a field whose name begins with _. We tried both with scripting disabled: named password, the guess was in the page source; named _password, the box comes back empty.

javaScriptEnabled: false is the cheapest progressive-enhancement test there is: one line, and the browser behaves like a phone whose script never arrived. The last assertion reads the whole page source, not just the input: the input is only the most obvious place the guess could travel, and reading everything the server sent catches it wherever it went.

Signing out is a form too

A form with no schema, because there is nothing to send: the button is the whole form. It is a real POST, so it signs you out with JavaScript off, and it ends in redirect(303, '/'), which a form is allowed to do. A successful submission with no refreshes of its own also re-runs every load function, so the header's "Ada Willow" turns into "Sign in" without anybody reloading.

A command cannot redirect

This was a command — onclick={() => void signOut()} — and it was broken in a way no test noticed. The SvelteKit docs are plain about it: redirect(...) works inside query, form and prerender, and "It is not possible inside command functions". In the browser, a command whose response is a redirect throws remote_command_redirect. So the session was deleted and the cookie cleared, and then the page threw, leaving the dashboard on screen with the owner's name still in the header. Two end-to-end tests now press Sign out, with and without JavaScript, and the shared fixture fails any test whose page throws an error nothing caught.

Fusing two answers into one field

The booking form has an interesting problem. The customer picks a time, but a time on its own is not bookable — it belongs to a particular staff member, and when the customer chose "anyone", the app picked for them.

The obvious design is a radio group of times plus a hidden staffId, updated by JavaScript when the selection changes. That design needs JavaScript. Without it the hidden field keeps whatever the server rendered — for "anyone", nothing — and the form fails validation for a reason the customer can neither see nor fix.

So the value carries both, and the schema splits it apart again:

Why the regex before the transform

The pipe runs in order. Validate the shape first, then split — so the handler receives a proper { start: number, staffId: string } and can never be reached with NaN or half a selection. Splitting first and validating the pieces afterwards means writing two error messages for one mistake.

The result: a customer with JavaScript disabled posts a complete, coherent choice using nothing but a radio button. Progressive enhancement that is genuinely progressive, rather than a fallback nobody ever tried.

One form per row

The services page renders an edit form for every service. They cannot share one form() instance — a pending state or an error on one would appear on all of them.

form.for(id) gives each row its own instance with its own fields, issues and pending count, all driving the same server handler. It is the difference between one spinner spinning and eleven.

{const editForm = $derived(saveService.for(entry.id))} is a declaration tag: a const written straight into the markup. Declaration tags arrived in Svelte 5.56 and made the older {@const} legacy. The $derived keeps the reactivity {@const} had — the value is worked out again whenever something it reads changes — where a bare {const editForm = saveService.for(entry.id)} is worked out once, when the row is created, like a const in the script. A declaration tag is visible to its siblings and their children in the same lexical scope: here that is the body of the {#each}, so each row has its own editForm, the snippets inside its <Field>s can read it, and nothing outside the loop can.

class={['card', { inactive: !entry.isActive }]} is the other idiom in that block, and every conditional class in this app is written that way. Since Svelte 5.16 the class attribute takes an array or an object and joins it the way the clsx library does: strings are kept, falsy values dropped, and an object contributes each key whose value is truthy. The older spelling, class="card" class:inactive={!entry.isActive}, still works, and the Svelte docs now steer you away from it — the attribute "is more powerful and composable". One attribute can mix fixed names, props and conditions, as the Button component does with class={['btn', variant, size, { full, loading }]}, where the directive needed a string template and two directives beside it.

Notice the second argument again, this time on a text input. as('text', entry.name) renders each row's form already holding that row's current name, and it is also the value the field goes back to if the form is reset. editForm.result is whatever the handler returned, so { saved: true } from the server becomes the "Saved." message on that one card and no other.

Checkpoint

Disable JavaScript in your browser, book an appointment end to end, and get a real confirmation page — chapter 25 shows how every step before the time became a link, which is what makes that possible. Then submit a bad email and see the error come back attached to the right input. Still without JavaScript, sign in with the wrong password: the sign-in form comes back with the email filled in, the password box empty, and nothing you typed in the page source. Sign in properly and press Sign out: you land on the home page, signed out. pnpm test:e2e does all of it with scripting switched off.
